---
title: "distance metrics"
---

## why distance matters

- many models and algorithms reduce to a notion of "how similar are these two points" — knn, k-means, dbscan, kernel methods, and anomaly detection all depend on a distance function
- the choice of metric encodes assumptions about what "similar" means; a bad choice can make an otherwise good algorithm fail, especially as dimensionality grows — see [curse of dimensionality](curse-of-dimensionality.qmd)

## common metrics

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| metric | formula (between $x$ and $y$) | notes |
|---|---|---|
| euclidean | $\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i-y_i)^2}$ | straight-line distance; sensitive to feature scale |
| manhattan (l1) | $\sum_i \lvert x_i-y_i\rvert$ | sum of axis-aligned steps; more robust to outliers than euclidean |
| minkowski | $\big(\sum_i\lvert x_i-y_i\rvert^p\big)^{1/p}$ | generalises euclidean ($p=2$) and manhattan ($p=1$) |
| cosine distance | $1-\dfrac{x\cdot y}{\lVert x\rVert\lVert y\rVert}$ | measures angle, not magnitude; common for text/embeddings |
| hamming | fraction of positions where $x_i\neq y_i$ | for categorical or binary features |
| mahalanobis | $\sqrt{(x-y)^\top s^{-1}(x-y)}$ | accounts for feature scale and correlation via the covariance matrix $s$ — see [covariance matrix](covariance-matrix.qmd#geometry--mahalanobis-distance) |

:::

## choosing a metric

- euclidean distance assumes features are on comparable, roughly independent scales — standardise features first (see [feature engineering](../training-evaluation/feature-engineering.qmd#scaling--transformations)), or use mahalanobis distance, which builds the correlation structure in directly
- cosine distance is preferred when only the direction of a vector matters, not its length — common for high-dimensional sparse data like text (tf-idf) or learned embeddings, where raw magnitude can reflect document length rather than meaning
- manhattan distance is often more robust in high dimensions than euclidean, since it accumulates absolute rather than squared differences
- hamming distance is the natural choice for categorical or binary features, where "how far apart" only makes sense as "how many positions differ"

## practical considerations

- always scale/standardise features before computing euclidean, manhattan, or minkowski distances unless every feature is already on the same meaningful scale
- distance-based methods can struggle in high dimensions as distances concentrate — see [curse of dimensionality](curse-of-dimensionality.qmd) — which is a reason to reduce dimensionality or select features first
- a metric must be learned or chosen before fitting, not tuned against the test set; treat it as a modelling choice validated like any other hyperparameter — see [hyperparameter tuning](../training-evaluation/hyperparameter-tuning.qmd)
